title: Heat (H) - Mass and Temperature Dependency
topicTitle: Quantity of heat (H) - mass and temperature dependency
notes: **Heat is energy in transit:** Heat ($H$) is the thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference. It is NOT a property of a body - you cannot say "a body contains heat." A body contains internal energy; heat is the transfer of that energy.

**Mass dependency (H ∝ m):** For a given substance and temperature change, the heat required is directly proportional to the mass: $H \propto m$. Doubling the mass doubles the heat needed. This is because more molecules means more total kinetic energy must change.

**Temperature dependency (H ∝ Δθ):** For a given mass, heat is directly proportional to the temperature change: $H \propto \Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_i$ (final − initial). Heating water from 20°C to 80°C requires 3× the heat of heating from 20°C to 40°C.

**Combined relation:** Combining both: $H \propto m \cdot \Delta\theta$. Introducing the constant of proportionality - the specific heat capacity ($c$) - gives the fundamental equation: **$H = m \cdot c \cdot \Delta\theta$**

**Sign convention:** When heat is absorbed (temperature rises), $H > 0$ and $\Delta\theta > 0$. When heat is released (temperature falls), $H < 0$ and $\Delta\theta < 0$. The sign tells you the direction of energy flow.

**Units of heat:** SI unit is the **joule (J)**. The CGS unit is the **calorie (cal)**. Conversion: $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical calorie). Another unit, the BTU (British Thermal Unit), is used in engineering: $1\text{ BTU} \approx 1055\text{ J}$.

**Heat vs. Temperature:** Temperature ($\theta$) is an intensive property - it doesn't depend on the amount of substance. Heat ($H$) is extensive - it depends on mass. A cup of water at 80°C has a higher temperature than a bathtub at 50°C, but the bathtub has more thermal energy (and more heat to transfer if cooled).

**Heat vs. Internal Energy:** Internal energy ($U$) is the total energy stored in a system's molecules. Heat ($H$) is the energy TRANSFERRED. When you heat a body, its internal energy increases: $\Delta U = H$ (at constant volume, no work done).

**Real-world analogy:** Think of water flowing from a high tank to a low tank. Temperature is like water level (height), heat is like the amount of water that flows. Two tanks at the same height have the same temperature, but the larger tank has more water (more heat capacity).

**Calorimetry context:** In all calorimetry problems, the equation $H = mc\Delta\theta$ is applied to EACH substance separately. Hot body: $H_{lost} = m_h c_h (\theta_h - \theta_{eq})$. Cold body: $H_{gained} = m_c c_c (\theta_{eq} - \theta_c)$. Set $H_{lost} = H_{gained}$.

**Common values of c (for reference):** Water: $c = 4200\text{ J/kg·K}$. Ice: $c = 2100\text{ J/kg·K}$. Copper: $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$. Aluminum: $c = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$. Iron: $c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$. Lead: $c = 130\text{ J/kg·K}$. Higher $c$ means more heat needed per degree.

**Why water is special:** Water has the highest specific heat among common liquids ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$). This means it absorbs huge amounts of heat with minimal temperature change - why it's used as a coolant in car radiators, power plants, and why coastal climates are moderate.

**Quick estimation rule:** For a 1 kg mass of water, raising temperature by 1°C requires 4200 J. So heating 2 kg by 50°C requires $H = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420{,}000\text{ J} = 420\text{ kJ}$. This is roughly the energy in 100 g of sugar.

**Power and heat rate:** If heat is supplied at a constant rate (power $P$), then $H = Pt$. So $Pt = mc\Delta\theta$, which gives $\Delta\theta/t = P/(mc)$. A 1500 W kettle heats 1 kg of water at $\Delta\theta/t = 1500/(1 \times 4200) = 0.357\text{ °C/s}$.
confusion: ❌ Heat and temperature are the same thing. ✅ Temperature is the average molecular kinetic energy (intensive). Heat is the total energy transferred (extensive). A spark at 2000°C has tiny heat content; a bathtub at 40°C has huge heat content.

❌ A body "contains" heat. ✅ A body contains internal energy (kinetic + potential of its molecules). Heat is the TRANSFER of energy due to temperature difference. Once energy is in the body, it's no longer "heat." Think of it like "payment" - once received, it's no longer a payment; it's just money in your account.

❌ All materials heat up at the same rate with the same power. ✅ Different materials have different specific heats. 1 kW heats 1 kg of aluminum ($c=900$) much faster than 1 kg of water ($c=4200$). The aluminum's temperature rises ~4.7× faster.

❌ The formula H = mcΔθ works for phase changes too. ✅ This formula ONLY works when temperature changes WITHOUT a phase change. During melting (ice → water at 0°C) or boiling (water → steam at 100°C), temperature stays constant - you need $H = mL$ instead.

❌ Specific heat capacity depends on the amount of substance. ✅ Specific heat capacity is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the MATERIAL, not the mass. 1 kg of copper has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, same as 1 g of copper.

❌ Heat always flows from hot to cold, so a cold object can never lose heat to a hot one. ✅ Heat naturally flows from hot to cold. However, a refrigerator CAN move heat from cold to hot - but only by doing external work (compressor). This doesn't violate the second law.

❌ If you add heat, temperature always rises. ✅ During a phase change (melting, boiling, sublimation), added heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing potential energy), NOT increasing kinetic energy. Temperature stays constant during the transition.
practice: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2.5 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2.5 \times 4200 \times 60 = 630{,}000\text{ J} = 630\text{ kJ}$.

A 500 g copper block at 100°C is placed in 200 g of water at 20°C. If no heat is lost, what is the final temperature? Set $m_{Cu}c_{Cu}(100 - T) = m_w c_w(T - 20)$. $0.5 \times 390 \times (100-T) = 0.2 \times 4200 \times (T-20)$. $195(100-T) = 840(T-20)$. $19500 - 195T = 840T - 16800$. $1035T = 36300 \Rightarrow T \approx 35.1°\text{C}$.

An electric heater supplies 840 J/s to 2 kg of water. How long to raise the temperature from 25°C to 75°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420{,}000\text{ J}$. Time $t = H/P = 420000/840 = 500\text{ s} \approx 8\text{ min } 20\text{ s}$.

What mass of iron ($c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$) at 100°C is needed to raise 0.5 kg of water from 15°C to 25°C? $m_{Fe} \times 450 \times (100-25) = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 10$. $m_{Fe} \times 33750 = 21000$. $m_{Fe} = 0.622\text{ kg} = 622\text{ g}$.

A 0.2 kg aluminum calorimeter contains 0.3 kg of water at 20°C. A 0.1 kg copper block at 90°C is dropped in. Find the equilibrium temperature ($c_{Al} = 900$, $c_{Cu} = 390$). Heat gained: $(0.3 \times 4200 + 0.2 \times 900)(T-20) = 1440(T-20)$. Heat lost: $0.1 \times 390 \times (90-T) = 39(90-T)$. $1440(T-20) = 3510 - 39T$. $1479T = 6390 \Rightarrow T \approx 4.32°\text{C}$ - wait, that's too low. Recalculate: $1440T - 28800 = 3510 - 39T$. $1479T = 32310 \Rightarrow T \approx 21.85°\text{C}$.
universalFacts: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C - specifically from 14.5°C to 15.5°C, since water's specific heat varies slightly with temperature. The modern value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (exact).

Water's anomalously high specific heat ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$) is due to hydrogen bonding. Breaking these bonds requires extra energy, so more heat goes into the system without raising temperature. This is why oceans moderate Earth's climate.

The concept of "heat" as a form of energy was established by James Prescott Joule in the 1840s. His famous paddle-wheel experiment showed that mechanical work could be converted to heat, establishing the mechanical equivalent of heat: $1\text{ J} \leftrightarrow$ temperature rise.

Joseph Black (1728-1799) was the first to distinguish between "heat" and "temperature." He observed that melting ice absorbs heat without changing temperature - this led to the concept of "latent heat" and the caloric theory of heat.

Specific heat capacity determines how quickly a material heats up or cools down. Metals (low $c$) heat up fast; water (high $c$) resists temperature change. This is why a metal spoon gets hot quickly in soup, but the soup itself takes minutes to cool.
summary: Heat H is thermal energy in transit between systems because of a temperature difference; a body stores internal energy, never heat. For a fixed substance the heat needed is directly proportional to the mass (H ∝ m) and to the temperature change (H ∝ Δθ), so introducing the specific heat capacity c converts both proportionalities into the exact master relation H = mcΔθ with Δθ = θ_f − θ_i. The SI unit of heat is the joule, with 1 cal = 4.184 J and 1 BTU ≈ 1055 J. Temperature is an intensive property while heat is extensive, so a bathtub at 50 °C holds far more energy than a cup at 80 °C. Every calorimetry sum applies this equation to each body separately and then sets heat lost by the hot body equal to heat gained by the cold body and the calorimeter.
importantConcepts: Heat is energy in transit, not a stored property: a body contains internal energy U, and H describes only the energy crossing its boundary because of a temperature difference.
Mass dependency H ∝ m: doubling the mass doubles the heat required for the same Δθ, because twice as many molecules must have their average kinetic energy changed.
Temperature dependency H ∝ Δθ: heating water from 20 °C to 80 °C needs 3× the heat of heating it from 20 °C to 40 °C, because Δθ triples.
The constant of proportionality is the specific heat capacity c, an intensive material property, which turns the two proportionalities into the exact equation H = mcΔθ.
Sign convention: H and Δθ are both positive on heating and both negative on cooling, so the sign of H always states the direction of energy flow.
importantStatements: Heat flows spontaneously from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached.
The heat required by a body is directly proportional both to its mass and to the temperature change it undergoes.
H = mcΔθ holds only while the phase of the substance is unchanged; during melting or boiling a latent heat term mL must be added instead.
Specific heat capacity c is intensive, so 1 kg and 1 g of the same material have identical values of c.
The SI unit of heat is the joule, and 1 cal = 4.184 J for the thermochemical calorie.
importantTasks: Convert a quantity of heat between SI and CGS units and between calorie, kilocalorie and BTU, showing the multiplier used.
Given a mass, a temperature range and the specific heat capacity of a substance, calculate the heat absorbed or released.
Write a calorimetry balance for a hot body immersed in a cold liquid plus calorimeter and solve it for the equilibrium temperature.
Carry out a dimensional check on a proposed expression for heat before attempting any numerical substitution.
keyPoints: H = mcΔθ is the single equation behind almost every numerical in this unit.
Temperature is intensive and does not scale with mass; heat and internal energy are extensive and do.
Water has c = 4200 J/kg·K, which makes it an effective coolant and the reason coastal climates stay moderate.
Quick estimate: 1 kg of water needs 4200 J per kelvin, so 2 kg heated through 50 K takes 420 kJ.
In a real calorimeter the vessel also absorbs heat, so its heat capacity C_cal = m_cal c_cal must be added to the gaining side.
specialNotes: During a phase change the temperature stays constant while heat keeps flowing, so the sensible-heat term cΔθ cannot describe the process at all; use Q = mL instead.
Specific heat is not strictly constant: water's c runs from 4217 J/kg·K at 0 °C to 4181 J/kg·K at 15 °C and 4219 J/kg·K at 100 °C, though school problems treat it as fixed.
At constant volume with no work done, ΔU = H; if the body expands and does work, only part of the supplied heat goes into raising its internal energy.
Δθ is a temperature INTERVAL, so 1 K and 1 °C are interchangeable in size; only absolute temperatures differ numerically between the two scales.
Two bodies at the same temperature hold very different amounts of energy, so being at the same temperature is not the same as having the same heat content.
examShortTricks: Anchor every answer on 4200 J per kg per kelvin for water; if 1 kg of water appears to need less than 4200 J for one kelvin, a mistake has already been made.
Build the calorimetry balance around the unknown equilibrium temperature so that every difference stays positive: m_h c_h (θ_h − θ_eq) = (m_c c_c + C_cal)(θ_eq − θ_c).
Use the single conversion 1 cal/g·°C = 4184 J/kg·K instead of juggling 4.184 and 10⁻³ separately.
Read every question for whether it wants heat capacity C or specific heat c; if C is given, divide by the mass to get c = C/m before substituting into mcΔθ.
examNotes: Carried as a 3 or 4 mark numerical in almost every paper, usually the heat needed to raise a stated mass of water or metal through a stated temperature range.
The method of mixtures is a standard 5 mark question: a hot solid is dropped into water in a calorimeter and the equilibrium temperature is measured.
One-mark definition questions on the difference between heat and temperature, and on why a body cannot be said to contain heat, appear frequently.
Expect at least one unit-conversion sub-part, so quote the SI joule value first and the calorie value alongside it.
practiceQuestions: How much heat is required to raise 2.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C, and what is that in kilocalories?
A 500 g copper block at 100 °C is placed in 200 g of water at 20 °C. What is the equilibrium temperature if no heat is lost?
An electric heater supplies 840 J/s to 2 kg of water. How long does it take to raise the temperature from 25 °C to 75 °C?
Using the mass and temperature dependencies, explain why doubling the mass of a body doubles the heat it absorbs for the same temperature rise.
Why is it wrong to say that a 100 °C spark contains more heat than a 40 °C bathtub full of water?
